Mr. J. A. ROBB (Huntingdon) moved for:
All correspondence and reports relating to the closing of the customs preventive station at Vicars, Quebec; the opening of customs House office or preventive station at Frontier, Quebec, county of Huntingdon, and subsequent protest against the closing of the office at Vicars. Also for a return showing reports since 1912 of inspectors and collector as to the administration and ability of preventive officer of customs John W. Curran, recently dismissed, at Vicars, Quebec.
He said: Though this may seem to the members of the House just one of the ordinary motions for the production of papers, to the people of the township of Havelock, Howick, St. Chrysostome, and all that section of country that has been continuously served for the past twenty-six years by the Customs station at Vicars, it is a very important matter. Early in December, when the announcement was made that the preventive station at Vicars was to be closed, there was a division of opinion in the community. Conservatives pointed out with pride that this Government was economizing; others said: Our Government friends at Ottawa have at last recognized that we were right in 1910, when we sent a deputation to the Government asking for reciprocity, and they are now going to give us reciprocity by closing this Custom office, and they will continue to close others all alon£ this road. But a few days afterwards, when it was learned that the Government had reopened another office 3i miles along the road, and out in a field,, there was a hurried convention of the faithful Conservative friends, and resolutions were passed. and sent to Ottawa protesting against the closing of the office at Vicars. It might interest the House to know that	for	some years priorto	1882,	there	was a	preventivecustoms officer at Vicars. In 1882 the then officer,	Mr. Boardman, resigned,and Mr.	Arthur Roberts	was appointed in his place. Mr. Roberts lived at Frontier, and died in 1889. Alex. Fiddes was then appointed customs house officer there, and he held the office until he died in 1906; and if there was one man in that community more than another who was an active Conservative it was Alex. Fiddes. Not only was he a good worker himself, but he had a large family and connection, and they were all active workers whenever there
was an ©lection. Fidd.es held that office for seven years under a Conservative Administration and for ten years under a Liberal Administration. All that time he was undisturbed, and free to take part in elections at election time. In 1906 Mr. Fiddes died, and Mr. John Curran was appointed in his place. Mr. Curran held that office until it was abolished in December last. No reason was given to him why the office was abolished; all he received was an official letter from the Department of Customs at Ottawa, saying that there was no complaint whatever against him, but that the office had simply been abolished. Vicars is on a Toad leading direct to the United States. It is a .splendid road, and has recently been macadamized right up to the international boundry line, and it is along this road, where the Vicars office was, that all the automobile traffic and business from the United States goes. The new office opened at Frontier is 3i miles from Covey Hill, and it is not on any direct road leading to the United States. Whatever explanation the Government mav offer, I think they will have a hard time with their political friends in Havelock to justify the removal of the preventive station from Covey Hill to Frontier, unless it be that the Government are repentant and now wish to allow our farmers to trade undisturbed with the United States.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO RETURNED SOLDIERS IN CIVIL SERVICE.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. S. MIDDLEBRO (North Grey) moved:
subtopic: PREFERENCE TO RETURNED SOLDIERS IN CIVIL SERVICE.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, in all future appointments to the Civil Service of Canada, preference should be given to those properly qualified candidates who have served with the Canadian Expeditionary Forces in the present war.
He said: My object in placing this resolution upon the Order Paper is two-fold: First to elicit an expression of opinion from this House as to the advisability of [DOT]securing for those who have already enlisted a simple measure of adequate justice, and secondly to stimulate recruiting by giving publicity to the fact that those

who in future enlist will receive preferential treatment at the bands of this Government in the filling of all vacancies in the Civil Service of Canada.
We have been urging the citizens of this country, by public meetings 'and by private solicitations, and in every manner which we thought best, to give preferential treatment to those of our Canadian Expeditionary Force who are fortunate enough to return from the front. If it was a proper thing to urge private corporations and firm's employing labour to give that preferential treatment, we, certainly should set the example as a state, and the state has a splendid opportunity of so doing by filling all vacancies in the public .service with men from the Canadian Expeditionary Force. As all those who return will not be able to secure appointments in the Civil Service, we shall have to create a preferential class among them, and in doing so, no doubt we shall take into consideration the fact that those who have been wounded, but who after a certain period will be able to perform the duties appertaining to civil servants, should be given preferential treatment among those who have served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force. One naturally looks about for precedents in bringing up a resolution of this kind, hut if there were none, the tremendous sacrifices and the general upheaval of the .traditional order of things consequent upon the present struggle, would be sufficient justification for us to create .a precedent; but fortunately in nearly every country preferential treatment has been given to ex-soldiers and ex-sailors who have .served in any of the wars of their country.
In July, 1877, ia select committee of the British House o.f Commons had under consideration the following questions:
1.	"Whether a better class of men would be induced to enter the military or naval service if the prospect were held out to them of civil employment after a certain period of meritorious service.
2.	"What would be the effect on the civil service of the introduction into it in a greater degree than hereto of persons who have served in the army and navy.
In regard to the former they reported:
That there is reason to believe that if it were well understood that a considerable number of suitable civil appointments were to be given to soldiers when their term of service expired, the effect on recruiting would be good and some men of a better stamp might be induced to enter the army.
41 i	1
With regard to question No. 2 they reported:
That a preference should be given to exsoldiers and sailors for appointment to the different positions named in the said report.
A second committee was appointed in 1894 to report upon the results which had followed the recommendations of the first committee, and also to report what further measures were desirable for the purposes of extending the employment of soldiers and sailors to the civil departments of the State and for helping them to obtain service with private employers of labor. Among other things this committee reported:
(a)	That in annually sending back to civil life so many thousands of reservists the State contracts towards these men a moral obligation which it should not hesitate to discharge.
(b)	That it would greatly popularize the service in the army and improve the status of the soldier if serving with the colours can be made under ordinary circumstances a condition of appointment or employment in the departments of the public service.
Many other recommendations were made, all with a view of assisting ex-soldiers to preferential treatment in the Civil Service and other branches of Government employment.
*Another committee .in 1883, reported in favour of employing the army and navy pensioners in the outdoor .and non-clerical branches of the Civil Service.
In 1906 a further speeial committee of the British House of Commons which went into the matter very exhaustively reported among other things:
It is the duty of the state to set the best example in the method of treating its servants and it seems to us essential that is should at once take steps to carry out such important recommendations, and to place itself on at least as favourable a footing as regards its -employees as that of other employers.
We therefore most earnestly urge that definite instructions should be issued to the various departments that ex-soldiers and sailors are to be given a prior claim to employment in the various posts in the Government service to which we alluded, and to any others for which their services may be suitable. For we are persuaded that such preference, given as it is by many employers of labour and public bodies, is all the more imperative on the part of the State. We feel, however, that by this means only can the State relieve itself of the moral obligation which is placed upon it for those who have borne arms and endangered their lives in its service.
Some of the recommendations of this committee were:
1. That an association which would be financially assisted by but not under the control of the Admiralty, and the War Office, should be

created for the provision of employment for exsoldiers and sailors.
2.	That the Government should direct the various public departments to fill vacancies in the appointments detailed in appendices 2 to 5, and any others which may be suitable, by exsoldiers and sailors of good character, and that only in the event of such candidates not being forthcoming are the posts to be filled by civilians.
Among other recommendations of this committee were:
3.	All future vacancies for customs preventive men should be filled by ex-soldiers and sailors.
4.	That at least half the vacancies for outdoor customs officers should be set aside for ex-soldiers and sailors.
5.	That the majority of vacancies for assistant clerks should be similarly dealt with.
6.	That all established messengerships should be so filled.
7.	That county and burough councils should be urged to reserve a number of appointments for ex-soldiers and sailors.
So far as my research has gone, it has satisfied me that these recommendations have all been from time to time carried out by the British Government. I tried to learn what had been done by the United States Government after the Civil War in 1865. I find that the recommendations made by the American Government in 1865 are still part of the Civil Service regulations in force on the 15th of August last. After the Civil War, or, perhaps, before it was over, a resolution was % moved and passed in the United States House of Representatives, which was afterwards enacted verbatim as section 1754 of the Revised Statutes of the United States, as follows:
Persons honourably discharged from military and naval service by reason of the disability resulting from wounds or sickness incurred in the line of duty shall be preferred for appointments to civil offices provided they are found to be possessed of the business capacity necessary for the proper discharge of the duties of such offices.
That is still the law of the United States, and it is followed in the administration of jihe Civil Service. A resolution was passed on the same day, afterwards embodied in the law, and now appearing as section 1755 *of the Revised Statutes of the United States, as follows:
In grateful recognition of the services and *sacrifices and sufferings of persons honourably discharged from the military and naval service of the country by reason of wounds disease or the expiration of the terms of enlistment it is respectfully recommended to bankers, merchants, mechanics, manufacturers, farmers, and persons engaged in industrial pursuits to give them the preference for appointments to remunerative situations and employments.

It is gratifying to note that the United States, before making recommendations to others, first declared by resolution and by law that they would do that which they asked others to do. In looking over the Freneh legislation, I find that, at least since 1870, the year of the Franco-Prussian War, there has been legislation upon the French statute books giving preferential treatment to ex-soldiers and sailors, wounded or partially incapacitated when on service at the front. That law is in effect at the present time. On November 15 last the Chamber of Deputies passed a Bill on this subject, which, as it is very short, I ask leave to put on Hansard. I do not know that this has been finally enacted into law through subsequent action of the Senate, but I understand that it has been, and certainly it is not likely that the Senate would make any very material amendments to a measure which was passed unanimously by the Chamber of Deputies. A free translation of this Act is as follows:
Relating to the reservation, under certain conditions, of employments to the men in the Army and Nav,y invalided No. 1, or retired by reason of wounds or infirmities contracted in active service during the present war.
The Chamber of Deputies has adopted the Bill drafted as follows:
Section 1. The military men of the Army and Navy invalided No. 1, or retired through wounds or infirmities resulting from wounds or illness caught in front of the enemy shall benefit, for a term of five years, dating from the end of the hostilities, by a right of preference for the obtaining of all positions reserved b,y statements E, F, and G, annexed to the law of the 21st of March, 1905, whatsoever be their rank or the length of their services-such right of preference to be granted in the first place in favour of fathers of the most numerous families.
They may be admitted to the benefit of said positions, even though they had, on the first day of August, 1914-
The date of the order of mobilization of the land armies and navies.
-passed the age limit as it is determined for obtaining the certificate of professional qualification under section 14 of the rule of public administration of the 26th of August, 1905, amended, to be in force under section 60 of the law of the 21st of March, 1905.
Section 2. A rule of public administration, which shall intervene within three months after the enactment of the present law, shall determine the classification of wounds or infirmities allowing to compete for the obtaining of a position reserved according to the terms specified in the herein above section.	,
Such rule shall likewise determine the manner in which to obtain the certificate of professional qualification, and the conditions under which the candidates shall he entered on a special . list established for each position, by the commission created in conformity with section 70 of the law of the 21st o'f March, 1905.
Section 3. A right of preference shall be

granted to such military men as are provided for in section first of this law, to compete for the obtaining of positions not reserved by the law of the 21st of March, 1905.
The administrations provided for in statements E, F and G. annexed to the law of the 21st of March, 1905, as well as the industrial and commercial undertakings holding a monopoly or a Government subsidy from the Department of the Commune, shall determine such lists and terms and conditions of access to positions as are apt to be granted to said military men, and they shall notify the Minister of War thereof, within four months after the enactment of the present law.
Section 4. No industrial or commercial undertaking shall, in the future, be granted a monopoly or a Government subsidy, from the Department of the Commune, except on condition of reserving to military men, who are the object of this law, a certain number of positions to be determined by the specifications in which account shall be taken of the situation of the fathers of numerous families, as provided for in section 1.
Section 5. All provisions: contrary to the present law are repealed.
Adopted in Public Assembly, at Paris, November the 19th, 1915.

The effect of this Act is to provide that for the period of five years after the termination of hostilities a preference shall be given to military and naval men who have been wounded while on active service, and who are qualified to fulfill the duties gf the office in the Civil Service. That means that they shall have the right to make application for positions which are vacant during a period of five years after the cessation of hostilities. It also means that a preference shall be given in the preferred class to those persons who have the largest families, and, in the third place, it means that all public corporations which held any kind of monopoly or which have been granted in any way a public bonus are required to reserve a certain number of their positions for men who have been wounded at the front. I do not know that we could use that provision, because we are not in the habit of granting monopolies. It is true that certain undertakings have received bonuses, but whether or not it would be right to apply this provision to them and make it retroactive, I am not at all prepared to say. I do think, however, that we would be quite justified in making the provision that preference shall be given to the men having the largest families.
It would be quite impossible, of course, to make provision for all those who served in an expeditionary force numbering from
250,000 to 300,000 men, much less to make provision for all those who have been wounded, and it necessarily follows that we must make some selection from among them for the very limited number of positions in the Civil Service that will be open to them. Broadly speaking, those who will return may be divided into four classes: able-bodied men who shall not have been wounded or incapacitated, for whom situations and positions shall have been kept open by patriotic employers. These men would naturally receive preferential treatment after the other classes have been provided for. Second, able-bodied men who were out of work at the time of their enlistment, or who have been superseded in their absence, and invalided and wounded men similarly situated, who will recover after a period of convalescence. Third, invalided and wounded men who are unable to follow their previous occupations by reason of some disability, but who will be capable after a certain time to take up other work. Fourth, men who will be permanently disabled and unable to earn their living under any circumstances. I presume it would be impossible for us to make any provision for the latter class in the Civil Service; they would have to rely entirely upon their pensions.
I know that employment commissions for returned soldiers have been appointed by the various Provincial Governments. The object of these commissions, as set out in pamphlets distributed throughout the country, is to ask employers to give preferential treatment to the wounded men returning from the front, and who will, after a certain length of time, be able to attend to their ordinary avocations. But while we have appointed those commissions in the various provinces, I am not aware that we ourselves are doing the things that we are asking these commissions to do. In the province of Quebec there has been appointed an employment commission, of which the Hon. G. A. Simard is chairman. Mr. Simard has with him a committee of seven prominent men of the province, among whom I am glad to see the name of my hon. friend for Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-ville). This commission is doing good work in the province of Quebec. In all the other provinces similar commissions have been appointed under the designation of military hospitals commissions. It is our duty, I think, to pass a resolution of the kind 1 now offer, so that those who have enlisted will be entitled to a preference in the Civil

Service. Besides, it will be a great stimulus to recruiting if we show the men that we appreciate their efforts and sacrifices, by passing a resolution providing that returned wounded soldiers who, when convalescent, will be able to perform the duties of a civil servant, will receive preferential treatment at the hands of the Canadian Government.
The first and paramount duty of Canada t'o-day is the prosecution of this war to a successful conclusion. We are urging private individuals and corporations to reserve for returned' soldiers occupations previously held by them, and generally to give preference to those who have served - on the Canadian Expeditionary Forces. The State should he the first to set this example, and the way is open to the State through the medium of the Civil Service, and anything which we can in reason do now as a reward for those who have offered their lives in behalf of their country, and as a 'Stimulus to further recruiting, is not only justifiable but is a duty.
This is a fight for national life. If we lose, some one else will appoint our civil servants, but we will still have to pay them. If we win, those who fought for and retained for us our power of appointment should be the appointees; at any rate, they should receive preferential treatment. No citizen of the State performs a more noble act, or better measures up to the supreme test of citizenship, than he who offers his life for his country in the present crisis, and hence he is entitled to preferential treatment at the hands of the State. Those applicants for Civil Service employment, who could have, but have not, offered their services to the State, can not complain if preference is given to the man who was willing to sacrifice his life for the State at a time when the national life was at stake. Who is more entitled to a position in the gift of the State than the citizen who has been so maimed fighting for the State that he is unable to carry on his previous occupation, though able to fulfil the duties of a Civil Service official?	.
I am sure that every day the real meaning of this war is more forcibly brought home to us. Every day members of this House receive a list of casualties, and they look over them for the purpose of ascertaining, perhaps, if there are any casualties amongst men who have enlisted from their own particular constituencies, or amongst persons with whom they are acquainted. I find that there are 29 names

in the list of wounded to-day; the addresses of the men whose names appear in this list are as follows: Hants, N.S., Winnipeg, Man., Beamsville, Ont., Vancouver, B.C., Speneerville, Ont., Peterborough, Ont., St. Faustm, Que., Sherbrooke, Quo., Paw-tuckett, Rhode Island, Campbellton, N.B., Liverpool, England, Kamloops, B.C., Edmonton, Alta., Belleville, Ont., Halifax, N.S., Leeds, Eng., Norfolk, Eng., Fife, Scotland, Liverpool, Eng., Ratho, Scotland, Elie, Scotland, Stornoway, Scotland, Glasgow, Scotland, Maidstone, Eng. Those whose addresses are given as England or Scotland are those who were the first to take up arms: Englishmen, Irishmen and Scotchmen, some of them reservists, no doubt, who gladly and voluntarily enlisted at the commencement of the war and went with the first expeditionary force. This list of thirty wounded men in one day is the result of the ordinary normal everyday fighting on the western front. At this rate, over 10,000 men are wounded in a year, without taking into any account any pitched battles or special engagements. At this rate, in three years' time we should have 30,000 wounded soldiers to take care of, and I have no doubt that that is not half the number of men that we shall have to provide for in connection with the present war. So I say that it comes home to most of us as it has never come before, that we must do something to provide for these .men who will return from the front. Thousands of families after this war will appreciate as they never appreciated before the full meaning of the poet's words:
Oh, for the touch of a vanished hand.
And the sound of a voice that is still.
We cannot do anything for those who have fallen, but we can do something for their relatives; we can do something for those who are willing to offer their lives in defence of their country by providing that upon their return they shall be given a preference in the matter of appointments to the Civil Service if they shall be able to perform the duties of a civil servant-
The right hon. leader of the Opposition has said that this war has been a revelation in many respects. It has been a revelation in this respect; that notwithstanding the fact that we were living in an age of wealth, ease and luxury, we are glad to know to-day that the best traditions of the British Empire and of the British race have been more than upheld in the present great titanic struggle. We were apt to think perhaps that conditions

in the city of Paris gave ns a true insight into the character of the French people. But a snapshot of the city of Paris is not a photograph of France, and a photograph of France is not a,picture of the mind or the heart or the soul of the French people. You may photograph the materialistic exterior, but you cannot photograph the mind or the soul or the heart of the people. Only when a great emergency comes upon us do we really know the inner feelings and qualities of the people. I am glad to say that France, England and Canada have all more than measured up to expectations and to the best traditions of these races.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I think I make a very reasonable request when 1 ask for the affirmative opinion of this House-I hope it will be unanimous-upon the suggestion that after the war is over those who have served in the Canadian expeditionary force shall, other things being equal, be given a preference in the matter of appointments to positions in the Canadian Civil Service.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew): I am sure that the House has been very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) as well as in the matter of his resolution. The circumstances under which we now find ourselves have, in a way, made a new Canada- We view things from a different standpoint; we seem to have got closer together as a people. While doing our part in the great struggle in which we are engaged, we are knitted in a closer web, than ever before has bound us. The idea of altruism seems to have spread not only in this House, but throughout the entire Dominion.
We perhaps may have been taught the lesson, and it may possibly have been needed, that supreme selfishness is not the best characteristic of a people, and while each may have been going on his way for years, and taking his share of the general prosperity that seemed to have been given to this country in abundance, we may have forgotten what to us may seem to have been the smaller things and, amongst them, the well-being of those around us. After all, the ideal of a man ought to be to so conduct himself and to so treat those with whom he comes in contact, that when he is called hence the world will at least be a better place for his having lived in it.
The men who have been asked to go to the front should not only have our best
wishes and heartiest support but, what to them is more important: they ought to know that their families shall not want for any necessity while they are at the war. This is the first and supreme business of this Parliament after providing for the men who go to the front. We must begin by assuring the men at the front, or the men who are asked to go to the front, that while they are fighting our battles and doing the work that we ourselves might be called upon to do, those who are near and dear to -them must have, not as a matter of charity or generosity, but of actual right, everything they require while the bread-winners are at the front, and who are engaged in a work far more important than anything ever before conceived by the people of Canada. It must be remembered that our armies are composed not only of men from the ordinary walks of life:	mechanics, artisans, and
workmen, but that professional and business men are locking their doors, giving up their business, putting aside their ordinary avocations, forsaking not only what to them means a livelihood but considerable profit, and going to the front in order that we who are left behind may continue to enjoy those liberties for which our forefathers fought and died.
When our brave fellow-eftizens come back, should they be allowed to be objects ' of charity? Sir, no Canadian who goes to the front must ever be allowed to stand at the street corner and pass the hat for charity. He is entitled to be 3 p.m. taken care of by the state so long as he lives. It does, not tend to strengthen the fibre of manhood that a man who fought and bled for his country should live on charity, and no man who has courage to go to the front would want that. The duty of the Government, and of Parliament, is plain; we should put ourselves on record as being prepared to give the first opportunity to the men who have made this sacrifice. Heretofore we have passed Civil Service Acts, and we have appointed men largely on account of their being political warriors, but now we have an opportunity of giving our returned soldiers positions which they have earned because of duty courageously, ably, and nobly performed. As a nation we ought to rise to the situation without any question or quibble about it.
My hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) has referred to the provisions made in France, Great Britain, and the United States, and although we aTe not going to take an

example from Germany, still it may be noted that Germany has made provision for her retired soldiers. If you take a trip through that country, as you possibly will in a few years, after it is defeated, you will find that all along the lines of government-owned railways old soldiers are given positions at a comparatively fair salary, and the statutes of the different portions of the German Empire which own and control the railways, provide that these men shall' be entitled to the first claim on these positions.
We are all one in wishing to do this, and to do it properly. If we are going to do anything let us do it right; let us make the men who have gone to the front, and whom we are now asking to go to the front, feel that the State is with them, not only now when the State wants their services, but through the years to come.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO RETURNED SOLDIERS IN CIVIL SERVICE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while supporting the resolution and everything that has been said by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro), and by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), I won id like to suggest an amplification of tne idea. There are men taken from all walks of life who may suffer accident, wounds, or partial disablement, which will unfit them for the occupations they were formerly engaged in. It is quite possible that in many cases a man who has been engaged in some active, outdoor calling, and who has been disqualified for the pursuit of that calling, may be given a training or education that would fit him for some other calling for which he would be mentally, but not as injured physically fitted, and for which he had not been before educationally equipped. It appears to me that this is the time and the occasion when, if ever, the question of technical education should be taken up in a practical way for this specific purpose. I do not wish to debate now the general question of technical education, but there is no doubt that in existing circumstances many men who have become unfitted for their 'ordinary callings might well be given an opportunity to acquire technical knowledge which would enable them to become useful and selfsupporting citizens.
I am induced to bring this matter to the attention of the House because of a condition which exists in the city in which I reside. That city has established a technical school. It is ,of course, a very expensive establishment both to inaugurate and to carry on successfully, and in the

present financial stress, when it has become necessary to reduce expenditure along many lines, many of the citizens feel that the expenditures necessary to this technical school should, under the circumstances, be postponed until a better day. In all probability this school will have to be closed, or its usefulness will be very much curtailed, for lack of financial support at the moment. I do not wish to make any particular suggestion to the Government in reference to this school, and I merely mention it to say that here is an institution well fitted to do the work which I have suggested. The disabled soldier who might be a suitable person to attend that school and get the benefit of its training will not, as things exist now, be able to do so.

It is practically a municipal institution; but it is1 not under the control of the city council, it is under the control of the school board. I am only citing this ease as an instance of what could be done; and I believe that what is possible in that case is possible elsewhere throughout the country. Altogether aside from the advantage this education would be to the soldiers themselves, it strikes me that it would be of immense advantage to the country to enable these men to recover their usefulness and productive power. Otherwise, a valuable part of the population would not be useful, productive, creative, or indeed, would not enjoy life with satisfaction to themselves. I thought it might be a good idea to bring this to the attention of the Government.
Might I also suggest that an opportunity be given to the' disabled soldier to enter, not exactly the higher professions, but the school teaching profession, for example. If the disabled soldier, who in his previous career did not have the opportunity of acquiring that degree of education that would fit him for school teaching or some kindred occupation, were given the opportunity of acquiring that broadening of knowledge that wduld enable him to become useful in this line, not only would his condition be better, not only would the country be discharging those obligations that my two hon. friends have already spoken of, but the country at large would be benefited by

the useful endeavours of a number of its valuable citizens, who, left to themselves, and without outside assistance of some kind, would certainly pass the remainder of their lives with a minimum of usefulness to the community, and with very much less satisfaction to themselves.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO RETURNED SOLDIERS IN CIVIL SERVICE.
speechtext:
I should like to remark that I have had some experience in this matter.
In my humble judgment, the suggestions of this kind that are being made from time to time, fall far short of the requirements. From the discussion to-day, it appears that only those who have gone to the front and have returned, are to be dealt with. What are you going to do with those who have offered and have not been accepted? Their effort, so far as it goes, is of immense value to the country, for by their example they are nourishing the spirit of self sacrifice and of defence-something which is most material. Furthermore, apart from the pension, what provision is to be made foT the permanently disabled, and the dependents of those who have been killed? To my mind the various schemes that have been suggested partake largely of the spirit of tutelage or guardianship, and have in them something which is not conducive to the best interests of the soldiers, their wives, and their families. I am well aware that there is a variety .of schemes in other countries, where the old soldier in many cases is treated pretty much as a sort of poor relation-somebody who has to be provided for. To my mind this matter should be dealt with differently, and I would venture to suggest a satisfactory method. The soldier is a man who offers his services in an enterprise of a peculiarly hazardous kind, requiring in him not only physical but moral qualities. You are paying that man accordingly, in the first instance. In the second place, I say you should insure his life. Then, if he dies, the insurance money will enure to the benefit of his family, and can be taken care of by trustees. If he is wounded, he can be taken care of- on the principle of the Workmen's Compensation Act, which provides for every degree of disablement. Under this plan, the old soldier would not be a pensioner upon public bounty, but a man whose business affairs would be on a proper business basis. This would be recognizing soldiering as a calling of the nation at large. It is just the same as any other calling, except that it differs in its
greater danger, and in other qualities of a like kind.
A soldier should be sent forth to war on the understanding that he will be allowed sufficient to properly provide for his family while he is away; and if he dies ui the service of his country he should be assured -not by the promises of the people, which are often written in water, but by a guarantee at the time of his enlistment-that when he enlists his life is insured, and that his future, and the future of his family is also assured. There are some cases arising out of this discussion which are not provided for. For instance, if a man is not fit he cannot be taken into the Civil Ser- [DOT] vice, and that man might have become unfit purely through the extraordinary character of his services to his country- I know a young man from Peterborough who holds the Cross of St. George from the Czar, the Legion of Honour from the French Republic, and the D.C.M. from England. He was shattered by shrapnel, by bullet and by high explosive shell; he was stabbed three times through the groin by a German bayonet; he was left out on the field to die. Even in that extremity, he gave up his stretcher to another man, in that way exemplifying the highest quality that the human race is capable of. He is now gradually degenerating; his mother was sent over to the Old Country to see him, but the young fellow's mind is gradually weakening. Am I, Sir, to understand that such a case is to be provided for in the way proposed in this resolution? This man is incapable of holding a position in the Civil Service, and yet nothing, apparently, can be done for him, unless through the spirit of benevolence of some charitable association, organization, or private individual.
I think, Sir, that this matter ought to be reduced to a thorough business basis, and, outside of that, there is ample room for those nobler qualities, shown in the volunteer and in the people at large, which it is so wholesome for the people to exemplify.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO RETURNED SOLDIERS IN CIVIL SERVICE.
speechtext:
It
occurs to me that one little thing might be done by us which would indicate our attitude towards this question. In this country there are those who have a certain say as to who shall be appointed to some of the smaller positions that do not come under the Civil Service Act, and I think it would be proper for us to make it clearly understood that those positions should be filled by returned soldiers who were capable of

filling them, and, if there are no returned soldiers available, we should take into consideration those whose boys had volunteered to take their places in the firing line.
One of the most pleasant duties I had in the way of nominating a man and having him appointed to a position in my county, occurred in this way. The case was a rather pathetic one * a woman was mourning the loss of her second boy, word haviiig just been received from France that he had been killed. It so happened that there was a vacancy in the Civil Service, and it was given to one son living at home who was partly crippled, but who was able to do the work required. I refer to this matter only to show the effect it had on every one who heard about it. People said that a very good effect was produced in Stormont by the fact that the position was given to the surviving son of this poor widow, whose other two sons had been killed. In any event, we should take into consideration the families of those who are fighting, and as far as possible appointments to positions in the Civil Service should be maue from the relatives of those who are serving us at the frpnt.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO RETURNED SOLDIERS IN CIVIL SERVICE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no objection whatever to the present resolution, that soldiers returning from the front, especially those who have been wounded, be given appointments in the Civil Service. But I would request the Government to see to it that the appointments go to deserving individuals, who not only will have the credit of having taken part in the war, but who, at the same time, will be trustworthy, and not to men of the stamp of those who have pillaged the House of Commons during the tragic conflagration of a few days past.
On that occasion certain individuals were about, who, far from deserving of their country, were unworthy of the military uniform they wore. They were more intent on barring the way to those who wanted to give aid and might have helped to save some lives than on fulfilling their duty.
An inspection of the ruins will disclose signs of plundering worthy of bandits.
I fully concur in the motion of the horn, member, provided a judicious selection is made; I mean that only those secure appointments who can be in every way recommended. Whoever offers his life on 'the battlefield-especially if he be wounded, de-	'
serves, on his return, the best consideration of, the Government.
With those few remarks I take pleasure in seconding the motion of the hon. member.	.

EMBARGO UPON OATS AND OATMEAL. On the Orders of the Day:

It has been reported in the papers that an embargo has been placed upon the exportation of oatmeal from Alberta to the United States. I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if there is any foundation for the report; and also whether any embargo lias been placed upon oats.

I think I can tell my hon. friend that no embargo has been placed upon the exportation of oats. If any embargo has been placed on oatmeal, it is a general embargo, not particularly applicable to any one province. I am not certain about that, however; I will give my hon. friend the information at the next sitting. I may add that there is no embargo upon the exportation of oatmeal to the United States; there is a general embargo in respect of its exportation to certain countries.
On the motion of Sir Thomas White for Committee of Supply:

I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to bring to the attention of the Minister of Militia and of the Government the matter to which I referred a few moments ago. I was saying that if it be true that the horses purchased in the other provinces of Canada were suitable and satisfactory, Mr. DeWitt Foster should still be in this House. 1 
say that the answer "Yes" to the question which I asked in that respect is not correct. More than that, the newspaper reports of the evidence heard before the Davidson Commission, if they may he relied upon, prove that that answer is incorrect.
I asked what commission was paid to the men who purchased the horses in Prince Edward Island, and the answer was that no commission was paid to them. I am pretty sure that is not correct. If I may rely upon the newspaper reports of the evidence before the Davidson Commission, some remuneration or commission was paid, and very properly so. The amount was a reasonable one, and the work was well done; the horses were suitable, and everything was proper. Therefore it seems clear that the formal answer given by the minister was not correct. There is a principle behind this. Members of this House have a right to ask questions in regard to public matters; the people of Canada have a right to information of that kind obtained through their representatives, and the duty of the Government to give correct answers to such questions cannot be disputed. Pains should be taken to see that every answer given in this House is correct. In this respect we have some complaint against the Militia Department. It may be that the department, being a military department, think they should not take so much notice of civil matters; or it may be that, the minister considers that everything he does ought to go without question;, but in any case we have some ground for complaint, and I am sure the Prime Minister will see that this grievance is remedied. I would ask him to tell me whether I should ask this question again or whether he will see that a correct answer is given without my again placing it on the Order Paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As the hon.
junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) is not present, perhaps it would be better not to go on with my estimates.

We might allow an item to stand.
Commission for payment of interest on public debt, purchase of sinking funds, $80,000.

What is the explanation
of the increase of $20,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is on account of the growing public debt, owing to the war borrowings. The department thought it wise to insert this estimate of $20,000 additional on the assumption that that amount would cover all possible contingencies.
Would the minister object to allowing that to stand until Mr. Maclean is here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was my
suggestion, to allow these items to stand. Item stands.
Removal of foreign and uncurrent coin from circulation, $15,000.

I presume that this is for the removal of American coin from circulation in Canada. Has the minister ever approached the United States Government with a view to having them grant similar accommodation to our coin in the United States? In Boston, for instance, Dominion notes or Dominion silver coins do not pass as current coin. Would it not be reasonable to ask them to give to our money the same accommodation as we give to theirs? That would be to their advantage, as we are their best customers, and I feel sure there is a disposition in the United States to promote intercourse with Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter has not been taken up with the Government of the United States,' nor do I think it desirable that it should be. The coin of neither country has any legal status in the other. The coin of the United States is not legal tender in Canada, nor is the coin of Canada legal tender in the United States. Along the border, and I think generally in Canada, American coins are taken at their face value. Under the arrangement referred to in this item, American coinage is taken up by the banks, to whom the Government pay a commission, and sent out of the country. It is to the advantage of Canada to have its own coinage in circulation in Canada, as there is an increase 
of Government currency to that extent. If the silver currency of Canada were replaced in whole or in substantial part by silver currency of the United States, to that extent Dominion currency would not be in circulation, and there would be a loss to the Government. Therefore, under the late Government, an arrangement was made by my predecessor, Hon. Mr. Fielding, whereby, in consideration of the payment of a small commission, the banks undertook to transport to the United States American silver and other coins, with the idea of getting rid of this foreign circulation. It is a fact that our coins do not circulate generally in the United States. I believe that in the American border cities our coins are accepted. I do not think it would be a proper subject on which to approach the Government of the United States. It would be for them to deal with the matter, if they see fit, as the Canadian Government has seen fit to deal with it. I should doubt very much whether they would meet any wish we might express to them in the matter. I think it better to leave the question to be dealt with according to the discretion of the Canadian Government on the one hand and of the American Government on the other, without any request on the part of either Government. To put forward a request and have it refused might be somewhat invidious. My own view is that, as trade increases between the two countries, probably our coins will be more and more acceptable across the line; and the Americans may in time adopt a similar plan to ours to get our coins out of their country. As we take the attitude that it is not in the interest of Canada to have American coins circulate in our country, I do not think the United States Government would take the attitude that the amount of Canadian coinage current in the United States should be increased. They would probably take the same view as was taken by my predecessor, namely, that it is advisable that Canadian coinage should find its way out of the United States, in order that the United States Government might have the advantage of the circulation of American coinage there.
Is this $15,000 a fair payment for the services rendered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the
amount paid out, according to this statement, on the commission basis, and, of course, no more is paid out than is required under that arrangement.
Is it confined to American silver, nickel and copper coinage?

The number of officials is the -same.

While the vote and the number of officials are the same as last year, merely with the statutory increases, I think that the minister will' admit that in view of the falling off of the business of the department that has occurred, there might have been occasion found of permitting the staff at any rate to decrease, as it must necessarily decrease, from natural causes. I do not see how we could very well do that. A great many of the officials of the inside service in the Department of the Interior have enlisted and gone to the front. The explanation of the minister is that the number of officials actually rendering service in the department has been decreased by enlistment.
Yes.

Is that common to all

Is the minister sure

Yes.

speechtext:
That was the rule up to
the 1st November.
What is the rule now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
An individual can only
enlist with the permission of the head of the department, who decides whether his services can be dispensed with. If his services can be dispensed with and he enlists he will be paid an amount equal to the difference between his military pay and the .pay he was receiving in the department, so that he will get the full amount of the pay he was receiving in the department.
Suppose his military pay is greater?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Then the department does not pay him anything.

How is it in regard to
many thousands of young men who are engaged in the outside service, and who, to all intents and purposes, are permanent employees? Are they to be treated in the same way?
The same rule prevails.
Is my hon. friend sure of that?
It does in my department.
It does in the Department of Customs.

I know a young man
who has been informed that if he enlists his salary will absolutely stop.

Well, this will take place, as it has taken place in one case in my own department. There must be some authority in the department itself who will judge as to whether it is possible

to dispense with the services of a civil servant or not, and if the civil servant is an indispensable one, as in many cases toe is, he does not then get the consent of the minister. In that case, not having the consent, if he enlists he does not get the same treatment.

Then am I right in saying that instead of their pay being allowed to go- on they receive a portion of their pay sufficient to make what they get equal to their former salary, and that the same rule now prevails in regard to the outside and the inside service?
Yes.
I understood the hon. Minister of Marine And Fisheries to say that the new arrangement was made on the 1st November. Was it the first of last November?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The first of last November.

Would the Minister of the Interior be good enough at some later date to lay on the table a list of the employees of the Department of the Interior, inside service, who have transferred to the overseas force, with the ranks they hold, the different units they belong to, and the positions they hold in the department?
Yes.

I would like to say a word about the enlistment of civil servants. I know of a few cases, not very many, where the head of the department has not seen his way clear to grant' certain officials permission to enlist. Like others who have applied to enlist, and who, for various reasons, have been rejected, these men are labouring under a little disability among their fellows, who think that they have not shown any intention of enlisting. I know some who have not made application for enlistment because they have been informed by the head of the department that they were believed to be indispensable. If some method could be adopted, either through their association or otherwise, of letting it be known that these gentlemen had offered their services and that they had not been allowed to enlist, it would relieve them from the effects of the feeling on the part of some of their fellows that they had not offered to enlist.

In my own
department there are two cases of that kind. My private secretary was very anxious to enlist and go to the front. To me he was indispensable, and I thought I was doing

some service to the country in carrying on the business that fell to my department. I therefore tried to persuade him that he was doing just as good service in remaining and assisting me as he would be doing if he went to the front. I offered to give him a letter to that effect, and I have made it public as far as it was necessary to do so. Another case of the same kind took place, and I offered to give this young man a letter which he could show to his friends. There has been some talk of having an armlet or some kind of distinctive badge to show that a man had offered his services, even if they had not been accepted. But I do not think any general application has been made for that idea to be put in practice in Canada. It is done in Britain, however.

A young man who has
offered to enlist and been rejected on account of being physically unfit would hesitate to wear a badge of that kind.
I suppose we shall have an opportunity of discussing the question of immigration. In regard to passengers crossing from the United States into Canada, the department has adopted a plan which is very convenient to the passenger, but which strikes me as not being quite efficient under the present conditions. For instance, a passenger from New York to Montreal or Ottawa is given a blank to fill in before he retires, so that the immigration officer will not have to rouse him out for inspection. That is a convenience to the passenger, and under ordinary circumstances, it would be sufficient protection; but at the present time, when it is very important that a great deal of care should be exercised with regard to those who are crossing the border, it seems to me that the present system is hardly adequate. I have often heard passengers on the train say, " I do not know how to fill this out," and get somebody else to fill it out for them, and then they would sign it. That might be all right in some cases, but in. another case it might allow an undesirable to get across the border. He could get some other person to fill out the blank, and could.go to his berth, and would not be aroused during the night. Does it not strike my hon. friend that at this particular time, when it is so important that undesirables should not be allowed to cross the border, even passengers might be inconvenienced for the sake of a stricter inspection. 1 think the present system allows an undesirable to get across the line if he has sufficient ingenuity.

I did not expect a question of this kind would come up on Civil Government Estimates. I may say that complaints have been made to me that the travelling public are put to a great deal of inconvenience by the officers requiring them to answer these questions.. Some hon. members of this House have objected strenuously to filling in these blanks, and have urged that the regulations be relaxed, as they were a source of great annoyance. I am convinced that our boundary inspection is much more rigid than it was prior to the outbreak of war. However, I will bring before the Superintendent of Immigration the point raised by my hon. friend, and see whether we can in any way *meet his wishes.

I know the present
system is a great convenience to the passenger. Sometimes, however, I myself have wondered why I should fill in the blanks, as no doubt have other hon. members. But there is ho difficulty in filling them out so faT as I am concerned, except that I invariably omit my age, which I suppose I should not do. In one or two oases I have had my own suspicions of people crossing the border so easily on the train. They simply filled in the blanks and retired, either to the drawing room or a lower berth, and were not disturbed at all. I think the present system leaves an opening for an undesirable to get in.
Most of the undesirables do not travel in that style. ,

The dangerous kind
travels in style.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have Had my attention directed on more than one occasion to the matter referred to by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). Usually it has been in terms of most outspoken complaint of the inconvenience occasioned to people of Canadian birth and residence by having to fill in these slips supplied by the Immigration Department. It seems to me that it is more or less a formal matter, and serves no useful purpose. I have heard complaints of this system by numerous people. Furthermore, most- men fill in these blanks in the most casual fashion, very often omitting to answer some of the questions, and treats ing the whole thing lightly, if not as a joke. If any undesirable wished to gain access to Canada I do not think these slips would interpose any formidable obstacle,
because the undesirable would fill in the blanks just as a great number of Canadians fill them in to-day, namely, in any such fashion as occurs to them. I do not look on these slips, therefore, as a safeguard against undesirable immigration. As far as I myself am concerned, they are an unmitigated nuisance, and I know I am expressing the opinion of the great majority of the travelling public in Canada when I say that. It may be that these slips serve some useful statistical purpose, and that compilations are made from these returns. But they do, undoubtedly, cause the people of this country a very great deal of trouble, and are looked upon as more or less of a farce by the railway companies who give them to the travelling public for the purpose of having them filled in. I do not desire to object to the system, because when a system is in force I suppose it serves some useful purpose, but I do not think it is in the public interest that any greater trouble should be given to the travelling public.

It would seem that stricter regulations are required at the present time. No doubt it is important to keep track of the people who come across the border. I notice by this morning's . papers that some fifty writs have been issued in the caise of San Francisco people who had plotted to come across the Canadian border and blow up bridges and tunnels, and commit other depredations. If the present system is not efficient I think the Minister of the Interior should take some steps to improve it.

At present he does not get as large a salary as some of the deputy ministers, who receive additions to their .salaries through some other employment or in some other way. If we are to get the best man for this responsible position, we ought, to make the salary a little higher than that which appertains to a deputy minister, or a least as high as the salary received at present by any deputy minister. I have thought of this matter a great many times, but this is the first opportunity I have had of presenting it when this estimate has come up. If any man ought to be well paid for the able and conscientious manner in which he performs his duties, that man is the Auditor General, and Parliament ought to give him a higher salary than the salary which he has received heretofore and which, I believe, is $5,000, the salary given to a deputy minister.

Let me mention another thing. In addition to the routine work, which has been heavy, and the responsibility which has devolved especially since the outbreak ot the war in connection with matters of finance, we have floated, as the House knows, a loan of $50,000,000 which was afterwards increased to $100,000,000.
The securities were in denominations of $100, $500 and $1,000. There were some 25,000 individual subscribers. And, notwithstanding that we made use of the services of some 3,000 branch banks of Canada, an account had to be kept in my department with each subscriber and of the bonds by number. I had some experience in connection with flotations when I was in business life, and I had then as good a staff, I think, as any man in Canada-I always stand by my staff. Yet I do not believe that any financial institution in the Dominion, no matter how great, could have handled that loan any better, in fact I do not think they could have handled it as well, as it was handled by the staff of the Finance Department. I am not paying any compliment to myself because I, as minister, simply supervised the issue in a general way; the compliment I am paying is to the staff, and I speak in appreciation of their work in connection with that loan as well as of the energy and the high sense of duty they displayed in the heavy work and responsibility which devolved upon them. I think it only due to the staff and to those in charge of the several branches that I should make this statement. And I have no doubt that ministers in charge of other departments could say the same thing. It is well known that the officials engaged in the Militia Department-to take that as an example-have worked literally night and day, Sunday and Saturday, since the outbreak of this war. Very heavy duties have been thrown upon these men, and very heavy responsibilities as well. If we were dealing with this matter on a business basis, or even on a basis of common fairness, I think the Government might well consider later on whether it would not be proper, just, and fair, that some remuneration should be made to these men who have put forth such efforts, and who have so untiringly devoted themselves

to their duties since the outbreak of the war. The same thing, I am sure, can be said of other departments. It is not necessary to enlarge upon this further, the point is, that men in charge of many departments of Government have heavy duties and responsibilities. And, in my opinion, they are not overpaid-many of them, I am satisfied, are underpaid. But we are at war. Men are giving up their civil occupations and are going to the front, making great sacrifices for the common cause. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is probably aware that in this issue, as in many others, there are two kinds of securities. There is, first, the bearer bond with coupons. This is what is called a negotiable security. It passes from hand to hand and the party who holds it, in ordinary course, has a good title though some of his predecessors in title may have found the bond or even stolen it. It is payable to bearer, both as to principal and as to interest. It is usual to provide that bearer bonds may be registered as to principal. That is, the name of the owner may be written upon the back of the bond, and in such case no one can deal with the principal of the bond except the person whose name is so written. But the coupons in such a case are not less negotiable than

before. So, in the case of the ordinary registered bonds, the principal can be dealt with only by the registered owner, while the coupons pass from hand to hand as if the bonds had not been registered. A record is kept in the department of registered bonds, showing the owner of each bond. When the owner desires to transfer his title to another, he does it by power of attorney, in which case either the name of the new owner is entered upon the back of the bond, or the bond is made payable to bearer. In the latter case its complete negotiability is restored.
There is another kind of bond, which forms a considerable p-rfrt of the recent domestic war loan. These bonds are registered both as to principal and to interest; they are registered bonds without coupons. In other words, the name of the owner appears upon the bond and in the -books of the Finance Department. If the owner of a registered bond loses this bond, he -can readily get -a new one from the Finance Department. Nobody else could make use of lost bonds of this kind if he found them or stole them, because, as I have said, they are registered both as to principal and to interest. In the case of the former bond, if it were lost and a diligent search failed to disclose its whereabouts, the owner would be required to file a bond by -a reliable indemnity or guarantee company guaranteeing the Government against any loss through the issue of a new bond. Upon a satisfactory bond of indemnity or guarantee being filed with the department, setting forth the facts with respect to the loss of the bond and guaranteeing the Government against its turning up in the hands of some innocent person who would acquire a good title, this new bond issues.
Does my hon. friend say it is a matter of law that a stolen bond gives title to the thief?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not to the thief. I say that a bearer bond has the quality of negotiability, under decisions. I can refer my hon. friend to some decisions; he will find them in Palmer's Company Law. In that work two or three leading oases are cited, in which it was decided that the character of negotiability attached to a bond payable to bearer.
I refer to stolen bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to that in a -moment. The quality of negotia-

bility means this: That a man who has a bearer bond, which he has acquired in good faith-even from a party who has acquired it not in good faith-takes title. Suppose the holder of a bearer bond has it stolen from him; there is no question that the thief has not good title to that bond. But if the thief goes on the open market and sells, that bond, which may be a listed bond, to A, B or C, who take it *v ithout knowledge of the fact that it has 'been stolen, then A, B or C take good title to that bond, because it has the character of negotiability to which I have referred.
