I wonder whether the Minister of Customs has apologized to the Chairman of the Board for the attack of last year.

Not at all. I do not take
back one word of what I said. I should like to add some more to it.

I do not see, then, how
the Government can collectively have confidence in the commission,-and either they should change the commission, or the Minister of Customs should apologise to the chairman, or resign from the Government.
I do not see how he can belong to a Government which has confidence in a commission in whose chairman the minister has not confidence. Personally, I think the commision has had a pretty hard row to hoe in many ways. I have differed with the chairman of the commission myself, but never in the language and tones of the Minister of Customs. I think the work of the commission is satisfactory on the whole.
I have heard that they have been overridden a good many times during the past year in their attempts to keep within the four corners of the Civil Service Act. I hope that is not true. I know the Minister of Customs would override the commission if he could; but I hope that the Government, instead of overriding the commission or endeavouring to get around the statute, will comply with it. It would be far better to improve the weak points of the Act than continually to appoint members to the Civil Service in violation of it. If I remember correctly, it is section 21 that proves most convenient to ministers who wish to evade the spirit of the Act. But there is a danger that they may go too far in applying that clause, which has reference to special or technical knowledge. I am glad the Government did not pay any attention to the Minister of Customs, and kept the commission intact.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Speaking in the House last year upon the subject to which my hon. friend has directed attention, I ventured the opinion that probably the observations which were made by the member of the commission alluded to bad been based upon the newspaper report of a certain return, and not upon the return itself. The gentleman in question came to me afterwards, and told ' me frankly that my conjecture in that regard was entirely correct, namely, that he had based his observations upon the newspaper reports, and he admitted in a very frank and manly way that he .should have looked at the return itself before he made his observations. Doubtless any Oivi'l Service Commission is liable to have more or less difficulties with any Administration. I do. not imagine, that the Civil' Service Commission has, within the same period, had many more difficulties with the present Government than it had with our predecessors. If some advantage has been taken of the section to which my hon. friend has alluded, I am very much afraid that my colleagues in the Government have learned a lesson in that regard from the example of their predecessors. I agree entirely, however, that while we have a Civil Service Act, it is most desirable that we .should conform with its terms, and make no attempt to stretch its provisions, or to use it for purposes which were not within the contemplation of Par.iiam.ent at the time the Act was pa.S'sed,

To my knowledge, Section 21 has been interpreted in .several ways. When I was Speaker, translation was declared to be non-technical. It has since been declared to be technical, and a large number of appointments have been made in that way; not only to the House of Commons staff, but to the staff generally. As to the personnel of the commission, if I remember rightly, a statute was passed about two years ago authorizing the appointment of a third member of the commission. That statute, however, seems to be a dead letter. In answer to a question put by me last year, the Government replied that there was no chairman of the commission; that both commissioners were on an equal footing. I think both members of the commission are hard working men, and that they have had a more strenuous time than they expected when they were appointed. Does the Prime Minister intend to complete this commission, or is the statute to remain a dead letter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think I was asked that same question both last session and the session before, and I give the same answer now that I gave then, namely, that we thought it was desirable to make some amendments to the Civil Service Act, that other matters in regard to it were under consideration, and that, pending those amendments, we thought it unnecessary to make the additional appointment. Mly hon, friend is quite correct in his

appreciation of the status of the two commissioners.

I should like to say a few words touching the Civil Service as regards the qualifying tests. I always laboured under the idea that a list was made of the names of candidates who came within the required number of marks, and that they had not to qualify further subsequently.
Only lately have I found out my mistake. It seems that all who come up for examination are put aside after there is found a sufficient number to fill the vacancies. To me this 'method of preference is altogether unfair. How 'does it work? Here are young men who have obtained more than the bare percentage of marks required. Yet if there be no position for them they are cast aside. They forfeit the fees they paid, and no more attention is given them than if they had never come up for examination.
In my opinion the system is unfair and should he changed. I should suggest, as a possible remedy, that a list be kept of all the successful candidates, and that they be not required, two or three years later, to pass further examinations.
It may be that some plausible justification of such a course can be found, but I fail to see any. Many complaints have come to me from young men in such a situation. I inquired the reason of their having been refused positions in the service. Their invariable reply was that they did not know. How could they know, when I myself, after five years in this House, and after ceaseless attempts to get information, am still in the dark. One of the Civil Service Commissioners informed me that of the successful candidates only the number required to fill the vacancies received consideration.
I hold that a change ought to be made. Among those who are rejected in this way some may be found who are as competent as those who secure employment. Yet they have to qualify once more, and undergo tests which are often very difficult, particularly for the first division of the Service, as well as for the second and third. It is most unfair to require of these young men to qualify anew on matters concerning which two or three years previously, when fresh from their schooling, they had successfully undergone the test.
I wish to discuss another question. My remarks, I feel certain, will not agree with 
a certain section of the people. I refer to the employment of girls in the Civil Service. In my opinion there are far too many in the departments. For a number of years some young women in the Service have been earning salaries reaching to a thousand, twelve hundred, fifteen hundred and even up to two thousand four hundred dollars. Those positions could be filled with advantage by young men who would willingly accept work at such salaries, come to Ottawa and become heads of families. To my mind the system is ridiculous to the utmost.
Those girls, if debarred from Government positions, would be none the worse fox it; they would become mothers of families, and thus the best interests of the country would be served. My four years' experience as member has brought home to me that those young ladies who receive large salaries are not anxious to marry. They prefer their salaries to household duties. Yet in motherhood they would be of much greater utility to their country. The Civil Service Commission might possibly do something to improve the situation. The matter, however, rests with the Government, and I appeal to the ministers who are now in office to bring about a change.
As I have only just stated, objection will be taken to my remarks in certain quarters, but I am speaking in the general interest.
There is another point on which I would insist particularly. In my opinion the number of French-Canadians appointed every year in the public service falls short of its due proportion, when the French-Canadian population is taken into account. Is it not beyond belief that in certain departments there is not a competent staff of translators?
My object is not to east any blame on the present Government. Similar conditions have long prevailed in the Service. It existed during the previous Administration, and it goes on to-day, because we have not sufficiently nursed the sore; we have failed to insist on having in the departments a fair proportion of French-Canadianp..
Last year I called the attention of the House to the fact that in the one department, on a total of ninety employees, only two were French-Canadian. I think it is unfair.
When we have dealings with the public officials we can hardly find any to understand us in French. In a room where are

to be found ten or twelve clerks, if information is sought in the French language, those clerks look askance at one another and appear to be at sea. It would seem, indeed, that our enquiries were made in Austrian or German.
If the Civil Service Commission cannot cope with the situation I call upon the Government to deal with the matter. Not the messengers only should be competent to speak French, but the higher officials as well. If such were the case there would be no renewal of the incident that happened a few days ago at the Department of Public Works, where a certain gentleman by the name of Narroway dismissed a French-Canadian because the latter spoke in French. It is sad for a French-Canadian to be told: No French spoken here, get out!
Again I. say that the Cabinet is not to be blamed for those conditions. The incident I referred to may be accounted for by the narrow-mindedness of the individual whose name is Narroway, but who would 'more properly bear the name of Narrowminded. I have about done with the remarks I intended to make on the 'Civil Service Commission.
Before resuming my seat I shall again insist on the fact that too large a number of women are employed in the Civil Service. I want the matter to be understood in its proper light. There are too many of these young ladies in the public service, who earn large salaries, and who, instead of putting their .money to a proper use, such as depositing it in the bank, or spending it to help their families, squander it in dress, so that it is of no benefit to any person, or to the country.
Departments Generally-Contingencies-care and cleaning of Departmental Buildings, including amount of $50 each to E. Snowden and W. H. Jeffery for firing noon gun, $220,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is an
increase here of $45,000. I had not expected to go on this afternoon, and so I have not the details of this increase before me; but my deputy explains that it is made in view of the occupation of the new Customs building in Ottawa, and possibly some other buildings as well. Of course, the House will understand, we are not bound to spend this $45,000. We will only spend as much as is necessary.

I imagine it is a matter which we need not discuss at this stage, but it has been proposed that the new
customs building should be prepared for the occupation of Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would make a difference, of course.

It would mean that the expenditure would come under another head altogether.
Referring to salaries authorized by statute, especially the item of salaries of ministers, after the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), I am more convinced than ever that the British system of giving different salaries to heads of different departments is not a bad system.
I am not sure that it can be worked out in Canada, for it seems difficult to work it out even in the case of deputy ministers, although there is considerable difference in the work of different deputy heads. At the present time, perhaps, we could not make a distinction between the work carried on by the different ministers, although to a person who has studied the situation, there can be no doubt that some heads of departments carry greater burdens and have to work much harder than others. I think that the country is growing so large that the Government will begin to think about the advisability or possibility of a distinction being made. But that is not what I specially wished to refer to. I call attention to the salary of the Solicitor General, $5,000. I understand that the Solicitor General is now a member of the Privy Council, a new departure having been made in that direction last year. Would the Prime Minister give the House an explanation as to how that came about?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Solicitor General is a member of the Privy Council; I think Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, when he was appointed Solicitor General, became a member of the Privy Council. It was thought desirable, in view of his position, and of his being occasionally required to discharge the duties of Minister of Justice, that the Solicitor General should be made a member of the Privy Council. Since becoming a member of the Privy Council he has performed important duties connected with the administration of the Department of Justice, which otherwise he could not very well have performed.

The Prime Minister has said that the HighCommissioner Iot Canada in' London is a member of the Canadian Government. I note that 'his salary is covered by this item of $10,000, though it

was not included in the estimate for the High Commissioner's office. I s'hotild like to have an explanation as to how this salary is made up, and how it differs from the salary given to members of the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Sir George Per-ley has been discharging his duties as member of the Canadian Government without portfolio. He is not in receipt of any salary.
But he gets this salary of $10,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. He gets an allowance for expenses, but no salary.
Why, then, are we voting him a salary?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amount was not expended last year, and it will not be expended this year.
Unless an appointment is made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amount is voted in view of the possibility that a permanent appointment may be made; but it is not paid to Sir George Perley. Being a member of Parliament, he could not receive the salary unless a change were made in the law.

As I understand it, Sir George Perley is a member of the Government without portfolio, and consequently he does npt get a salary as a member of the Government. His expenses are paid,
' but his services are gratuitous.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He receives only an allowance for expenses, and even about these he has been more ot less sensitive.
I have urged him to include certain items of additional expense to which he is subjected, and it was only with the greatest reluctance that he was induced to accept even part of those expenses which I thought were quite reasonable, and which I am sure Parliament would ratify.
Administration of Justice-living allowance for judge of Atlin district, B.C., $1,200.
Mr. MARCIL,: Great inconvenience is occasioned by the * non-appointment of judges to fill vacancies in the districts of Montreal and Three Rivers. Does the Prime Minister know whether it is the intention to fill these vacancies in the near future?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is upon the recommendation of the Minister of Justice that such appointments are made, but his unfortunate illness, which has lasted longer than he anticipated, has prevented the bringing of these matters to a head. I anticipate that he will be here toenorrow or Friday at the latest, when, no doubt, he will take up the matters to which my hon. friend has referred.
Legislation-Library of Parliament, $62,200.

I think it would be wise for us to have some authoritative statement as to the condition of, the Library. We have a good report in the press, of course, but I think it would be well to have the statement of the Government as to the condition of the Library since the fire.
Sir ROBERT |10RDEN: I am not quite sure whether the librarians have been able up to the present time to make such an examination as would give information of certainty. However, I shall ask the joint librarians to prepare at the earliest pos-. sible moment a statement embodying the information which my hon. friend asks for.
Is it the intention of the Government to have in this building a temporary library for the use of members during the session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have really not had an opportunity of considering that; I shall bear my hon. friend's suggestion in mind and ascertain whether or not it ils practicable. The reading room, I understand, is provided for. I have not heard from the Minister of Public Works as to the practicability of bringing any part of the library into this building. I am afraid that if we did bring part of it here it would probably turn out that the particular books wanted on any occasion were not the books that were here.
We might have the Hansard and the Statutes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand
from the Clerk of the House that arrangements have been made to provide a complete set of Hansard at once, and of the Statutes, as soon as practicable.
Legislation-contingent expenses in connection with the voters' lists, $10,600.

Is it the intention of the Government to print the voters' lists which are now being compiled for the current
year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it would take a great deal more than this amount to print the lists. I cannot remember at the moment that the subject was under consideration, but I shall make inquiry and give the information to my hon. friend.

I notice from an answer given the otheT day that a number of voters' lists were printed, not in Ottawa, but at various places in the Maritime Provinces. I think that was a departure from the usual way of printing the lists, and I should like to know what proportion were thus printed; the reason for resorting to that method, and if that printing was done by public tender.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will make
inquiry and give the information to my hon. friend. The Printing Department has had a great deal of extra work in connection with the war.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without motion put, pursuant to rule.
Thursday, February 10, 1916.
